genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the site manager learned her trade through an apprenticeship
her team works on old buildings
clients mainly ask for surfaces refinished from scratch
the footings give way under the storeys that were added
the floors are held on temporary props before anything else is done
the ground is surveyed to find hidden voids
the gaps in the masonry are filled only once the building is safe
she refuses decorative finishes while the frame is still fragile
she takes the client under the floor to show the damaged timbers
text: She came into the trade as an apprentice on renovation sites, and now runs a team that puts tired old buildings back on their feet. The same argument greets her on every job: owners want their walls smooth and freshly finished, while beneath them the footings are sinking under storeys piled on over the years. Her answer is a fixed order of work. Floors go up on temporary props before anything else is touched. Only then is the ground surveyed for hidden voids. Gaps in the masonry get filled last, once the place is safe to stand in. She will not lay a decorative finish while the frame is still fragile, and that stance costs her some distinctly awkward conversations. When an owner digs his heels in, she hands him a torch and walks him under the floor, where the timbers eaten away by damp speak for themselves.

units: two neighbouring buildings stand at the end of the same street
the first is entirely glazed and reflects the sky
the second is low and built of fired brick
the old front still carries the marks of the builders' hands
the tower is judged too regular in its geometry
the house offers worn thresholds and crooked corners
the old building is criticised for being cramped and decayed
the low rooms hold the heat better
the thick walls soften the sounds
text: Two buildings stand at the far end of the same street, and the taller one overshadows its neighbour without ever winning the argument. The first is glass from top to bottom; it hands the sky straight back at you, you admire it for a minute, and then the eye slides off it altogether. The second is low, heavy, built of fired brick that the weather has smoothed, and it holds the gaze. Its front still carries the marks of the hands that laid it. Set side by side, the modest one comes off better. The tower offers a flawless geometry, the old house crooked corners and thresholds worn hollow. One is visited, the other is lived in. People often call the old place cramped and decayed, forgetting that its low rooms hold the heat and that its thick walls take the edge off noise. Beauty here comes from use rather than from line.

units: the writer sends his sister news of the building work
three jobs are running at the same time
the broken tiles have been replaced by the roofer
the joints around the flue have been filled with a flexible mortar
every window opening has been made airtight
tape has been applied along the fixed frame of the windows
the builder suggests partitioning off the back room for a study
the partition will be lightweight board with no contact with the ceiling
the walls will get a limewash coat before the cold season
text: Dear sister, here at last is the promised news from the house. Three separate jobs are running at once, so I shall take them one after another. Up on the roof, the roofer has swapped out the tiles that had broken, then gone back over the joints around the flue with a flexible mortar. At the windows, I decided to make every opening airtight: foam squeezed into the rebate, tape run along the fixed frame, and the draughts through them have gone for good. Inside, the builder suggests partitioning off the back room to make a study; the partition would be lightweight board, stopping short of the ceiling. The walls still want a coat of limewash before the cold season sets in. I shall write again as soon as the roof timbers have been checked. Give the children a kiss from me when you see them.

units: the lead designer is asked to describe how the work unfolded
a detailed inventory of the existing fabric opened the project
that survey took a whole season
the examinations brought a weakened timber frame to light
the programme had to be revised after that finding
only the frailest part was pulled down
the rebuilding relied on the foundations that were kept
the cramped site complicated the organisation between the trades
bringing the pipework back into service was the trickiest phase
text: The lead designer is invited to set out how the work unfolded, stage by stage. She replies that it opened with a full inventory of the existing fabric, taken room by room across an entire season. Asked what followed, she explains that the surveys exposed a weakened timber frame, which forced a rewrite of the programme. On the technical choices, she says the decision was taken to pull down the frailest wing alone, and to rebuild on the foundations already there. Questioned about the obstacles, she points to the trades having to work around one another on a cramped site. Asked at last what she takes from so long an undertaking, she answers that the hardest stretch was not the structural work but bringing the pipework back into service, finished a long way past the date that had been announced.

units: a carpenter explains to his apprentice that the door is catching
the fault comes from the movement of the structure and not from the door
fitting another door would bring back the same jamming
a mark on the threshold proves that the settlement is continuing
the apprentice suggests planing the bottom of the leaf
the carpenter accepts this temporary solution
the bearing of the wall will have to be taken up afterwards
the catching will return if the ground drops further
text: The carpenter told his apprentice that the door was catching because the building itself had shifted. The apprentice asked whether it ought to be replaced. No, said the carpenter: the trouble lay in the ground, so a replacement would jam exactly as this one did. He pointed to the scrape the leaf had left on the threshold, proof that the settlement had not stopped. The apprentice suggested planing the bottom of the leaf. His teacher agreed, though he warned that the trick eased the symptom without curing anything, and that the bearing of the wall would have to be taken up afterwards. With the ground still dropping, he added, the door would be catching again within a season or two. The apprentice wrote the lesson down: treat the cause, or the repair keeps coming back, and the bill with it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old builders wanted to roof a wide hall without a central support
a flat stone roof breaks under its own weight
the solution adopted was to lean the blocks against one another
this form sends the load out towards the side walls
timber supports held the work up while it was being built
those supports were taken away once the central block was in place
the sideways thrust pushed the walls apart
masses of masonry were added against the walls to hold them
text: Picture builders who want to roof an enormous hall without planting a single column in the middle. Their problem is plain enough: stone is heavy, and a flat roof snaps under its own weight the moment you stretch it across. So they went looking elsewhere. What they hit on was the vault. Lean the blocks against one another and the load slides out towards the walls instead of dropping straight down. The trouble was holding it all up during the build, hence the timber centring slid underneath to carry the stonework until it closed on itself. Once the keystone dropped in, the timber came away and the vault stood alone. That left the sideways push, which shoved the walls outwards; the builders answered with thick buttresses. Neat, isn't it? Every obstacle called for one more piece, and the hall stood in the end.

units: the choice between timber and masonry depends on the use of the building
a brick wall stores the heat before giving it back
a timber wall warms quickly and cools just as quickly
the heavy solution suits rooms that are occupied all the time
the light structure suits premises used irregularly
masonry calls for drying time and a large workforce
the timber parts arrive cut to size and go together without water
the prices of the two methods end up meeting
designers advise deciding by the indoor feel that is wanted
text: Timber or masonry? The question comes up on every single project, and the answer turns mostly on how the building will be used. A brick wall banks heat: it warms slowly, then hands the warmth back as the evening cools. A timber wall behaves the other way round, coming up to temperature fast and losing it just as fast. For a room that is in use without a break, the heavy option wins. For premises opened now and then, the light frame comes out ahead. The building work divides the two camps as well: masonry has to dry out and takes a large workforce, while timber panels turn up cut to size and go together without water. The final bill, though, tends to land in much the same place. Designers therefore suggest choosing by the indoor feel you are after, rather than by the fashion of the moment.

units: an elderly tenant obtains a walk through the block before its demolition
the hall floor is damaged and holds the print of the furniture taken out
the doors of the flats are shut and marked with a chalk cross
a thin partition had already been broken into by the workmen
an old wall covering appears behind the split board
the roof timbers of the top floor let a draught through
the handrail worn by use moves her more than the rest
she thanks the caretaker as she leaves
she refuses to turn her eyes towards the front of the building
text: On the eve of the demolition, the oldest tenant was granted one last walk through the condemned block. She pushed open the door of the hall first, where the cracked tiling still held the print of the furniture that had been carried out. Then she climbed towards the landings, counting the closed doors, each one marked with a cross drawn in chalk. On the third floor she stopped at a thin partition the workmen had already broken into; behind the split board lay an old wallpaper nobody had ever scraped off. She finished under the roof, where the worn timbers let a thin thread of air come through. Nothing moved her more than the stair rail, polished smooth by hands that were long gone. On her way out she thanked the caretaker, then she refused to turn her eyes towards the tall grey front.

units: the crack must be raked out down to a sound backing
the dust is removed with a brush
the edges are damped before the filler goes on
the powder must be tipped into the water and not the other way round
the paste is pressed into the hollow to drive the air out
the surface is smoothed with a wide tool running past the sides
the drying lasts a full night at least with no heating
the hardened area is then sanded and dusted down
a mineral paint is applied in two crossed coats
text: Start by raking out the crack along its whole length with the tip of a trowel, until you reach a sound backing. Brush the dust out of the groove, then damp the edges lightly: filler laid on a surface that is too dry will simply let go. Mix the paste in a clean bucket, tipping the powder into the water and never the other way round. Work it in straight away, pressing hard so that the air is driven out of the hollow. Smooth it off with a wide knife, running a little past the crack on either side. Leave it to set for a full night at least, with no heating on in the room. Sand the hardened patch with a fine abrasive, dust it down again, and run a hand over the joint to check that the repair can no longer be felt under the fingers. Finish by brushing on a mineral paint, in two coats laid crosswise.

units: entry to several buildings in a low-lying district has been barred
the families moved out have been put up in a communal hall
a body of groundwater has been swollen by repeated rain
the sand carrying the foundations has been washed away by that water
the ground has settled unevenly
stepped cracks have appeared on the fronts of the buildings
the experts judge that the old fabric could not take such movement
the stairwells have been declared unsafe
resin injections are announced to avoid demolition
text: Access to several blocks in the low-lying district was barred yesterday, and the families moved out have been put up in a communal hall. The technical services have known the cause for seasons: a body of groundwater, swollen by one downpour after another, has washed away the sand on which the foundations sit. The ground has settled unevenly, opening stepped cracks across the fronts of the buildings. The experts called in judge that the fabric, decayed already, was in no state to absorb movement of that order. As a direct result, the stairwells were ruled unsafe and the evacuation was ordered without delay. Owners are demanding a second, independent survey, since putting matters right would mean underpinning the footings. The authorities announce resin injections, failing which demolition would become unavoidable.
